Triggers.value: Beginning to feel detached or unreal

Maladaptive Strategies.value: keep mind occupied all the time

Memory.value: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.

vignette:
Samuel is a man who carries his seventy-seven years with a quiet, almost unnerving stillness. A software engineer who still consults part-time, his mind is a place of logic and order, a stark contrast to the memories he has spent over four decades trying to contain. The trauma occurred when he was a university student in his home country, a place he has not seen since. It wasn't a single event but a sudden, violent tear in the fabric of his world. He remembers soldiers, the sharp crack of a door being kicked in, and the booming, indecipherable commands. The memory isn't a narrative; it's a series of still frames, silent and stark.

When he speaks of it, which is rare, his voice is flat, devoid of emotion. He describes the images as if discussing a photograph album belonging to a stranger. There is a picture of a young man's face, wide with terror, a friend whose name he has long forgotten. There is another of a soldier's boot, heavy and black, planted inches from his own hand on the floor. He says he can recall these moments with perfect clarity, but feels nothing, as if watching a silent film about someone else's life. Because that image of the soldier's boot is so sharp and fixed in his mind, he has become acutely sensitive to the sight of heavy work boots, a detail that now feels charged with threat and makes him scan the feet of strangers on the rare occasions he leaves his home. This detachment is both a mercy and a horror, leaving him feeling hollowed out by his own past.

The world is filled with echoes of those shouted commands. A recent trigger was an email from his project manager with a subject line in all caps: "ACTION REQUIRED." The sharp, authoritative tone was enough to make the images flash behind his eyes-the soldier's open mouth, the glint of a rifle barrel. This is the pattern of his life: an unexpected order or a news report about a distant conflict acts as a switch, and the silent slideshow begins to play in his mind without his consent. To preempt this, Samuel now meticulously filters his inbox, deleting anything with an urgent or commanding subject line before he can even open it, a small act of control in a world of potential mental ambushes. That sudden intrusion of the past is terrifying, a mental ambush he is constantly bracing for. He also finds that the first hint of a dissociative feeling, a sense of unreality as if he's floating slightly outside his own body, is now a powerful trigger in itself, heralding the return of the memories.

The return of these snapshots immediately activates a powerful urge to retreat. The sheer distress of seeing those faces again drives him to cancel plans and pull away from the world. If his wife suggests they attend a community event, the intrusive image of a crowded, chaotic room from his past surfaces, and he finds himself making an excuse to stay home. He has come to believe that safety lies in solitude and silence. The memories have also made him hyper-attuned to his own internal state; that feeling of detachment is particularly terrifying, as it feels like the very beginning of losing control, a prelude to the images taking over completely. He will do anything to avoid it.

To manage this constant threat, Samuel has constructed a life of meticulous avoidance. He rarely leaves the house except for groceries at off-peak hours. His primary strategy is relentless mental occupation. He spends ten to twelve hours a day in his home office, losing himself in complex coding problems and logic puzzles. He believes that if he can keep his mind completely full, there will be no empty space for the pictures to enter. This constant suppression, however, seems to have had the opposite effect. By never allowing the memory to be processed as a story, he has inadvertently preserved it in its most potent, fragmented form, ensuring it can only ever return as those jarring, silent snapshots.

His strategies have, over time, made him more vulnerable. By confining his world to the four walls of his house, his sensitivity to triggers has become more acute. A simple request from his wife to help with a task can now feel like a command, sparking a flash of irritation and a retreat to his office. His self-imposed isolation means that when he does feel that sense of unreality begin to creep in, it feels catastrophic, a signal of imminent danger with no one around to ground him. His attempts to control the threat have only made it more powerful, tightening a loop where his avoidance makes him more sensitive to triggers, which bring back the memories, which in turn deepens his need to avoid the world.

It was his wife who finally insisted he seek help. After he refused to attend their grandson's graduation, she told him, with tears in her eyes, that she felt she was living with a ghost. Samuel came to therapy not with any real hope of erasing the pictures-he is certain they are a permanent part of his mind-but from a deep, gnawing fear of losing the last connection to the life he had before. What frightens him more than the memories themselves is the prospect of being left utterly alone with them, watching the same silent, repeating frames for whatever years he has left.

violations.explanation: The vignette does not state that triggers directly cause maladaptive strategies; instead, it shows that triggers activate the memory, which in turn leads to avoidance.
The vignette does not state that the trauma memory leads to or creates new triggers; it only describes external cues and internal feelings as triggers.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies: The vignette does not state that triggers directly cause maladaptive strategies; instead, it shows that triggers activate the memory, which in turn leads to avoidance.
  e.g. "She stopped taking that route to work entirely — better to add twenty minutes to her commute than to feel that way again."
  e.g. "When the anniversary came around, she kept herself moving all day, cleaning, cooking, anything, because sitting still meant the thoughts would catch up."
  e.g. "She started leaving events early, telling herself she was tired, because staying too long meant the chances of something going wrong only multiplied."
- Memory → Triggers: The vignette does not state that the trauma memory leads to or creates new triggers; it only describes external cues and internal feelings as triggers.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
